issues_found: The 'pack camels' whose loss triggers defeat are CAMEL_RIDER units — armed military camelry, not baggage animals. The engine ships Trade Carts (and the Italians civ has access to them), which would have represented a merchant caravan's goods far more honestly; this was an avoidable choice.

Player 1's escort is 2 Knights, 3 Men-at-Arms and 3 Crossbowmen — a Latin-Christian field detachment. The Polos travelled as a small family merchant party with local guides and Khanate paiza protection, not with a mounted knightly guard; the composition would fit any generic 13th-century European force.

Marco Polo is a renamed KING, i.e. a crowned monarch figure escorted across Asia — visually and semantically wrong for a teenage Venetian merchant; a renamed villager, trade cart driver or generic hero unit would have been closer.

Elevation is uniformly 0 across all 120x120 tiles, so the 'mountain passes of Central Asia' named in the brief, in the objective text, and in the [D3] Mountain Pass trigger simply do not exist as geography. Six CLIFF_DEFAULT_2 objects are placed as decoration on flat ground, which cannot create the chokepoint the Pamir/Hindu Kush crossing turned on.

The map is a featureless sand sheet with one four-tile water pocket. The historical route crossed the Persian plateau, Hormuz, the Pamirs and the Gobi — no variation in terrain type marks any of these stages, so the desert-to-mountains-to-steppe progression the narration describes is unsupported.
Kublai Khan himself is not represented by any unit; Shangdu is a GAIA castle/town centre with yurts and a flag, so the destination court is unpeopled.
The three 'pack camel lost' defeat triggers all display the identical message, so the player cannot tell which animal was lost.
strengths: Player 1 is ITALIANS — the correct civilization for Venetian merchants, giving apt Mediterranean architecture for the caravan's tents and market.
Player 2 is MONGOLS with 6 Cavalry Archers, 4 Light Cavalry and a Scout — an accurate mounted-archer raiding profile for Central Asian steppe horsemen, and their yurt camp is culturally consistent.

The raider leader is named for Khaidu (Kaidu), the Chagatayid/Ögedeid prince genuinely in revolt against Kublai in Central Asia during the 1270s — a real and well-chosen antagonist rather than an invented bandit.

Victory is BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA on the unit renamed Marco Polo, reaching the Shangdu quadrant (90,90)-(100,100) — exactly the historical goal of the journey, keyed to the right person and the right place, not a unit hunt.
Defeat conditions are all specific to the caravan's actual vulnerabilities: the death of Marco, the death of Niccolo, and the loss of the trade goods — no generic 'all units dead' fallback.

The five narrative beats (oasis, ambush, pass, approach, arrival) are all gated on the escorted party reaching successive areas rather than on elapsed time, so the sequence follows the player's progress along the route.
Dates in the text are correct: departure 1271, arrival at Shangdu 1275, and Shangdu correctly identified as Kublai's summer capital.
justification: The scenario gets its factions right — Italians for the Venetians, Mongols for Kaidu's steppe raiders — and encodes precisely the historical goal, escorting the man named Marco Polo to Shangdu while keeping Niccolo and the trade goods alive, with waypoint-gated narration that follows the route in order. It fails badly on geography: every tile of the 120x120 map is elevation 0, so the 'mountain passes of Central Asia' invoked by the brief, the objective text and the [D3] Mountain Pass trigger exist only as six decorative cliff props on flat sand. Force composition is the other weak point: the caravan's trade goods are represented by armed CAMEL_RIDER units when Trade Carts were available, and the escort of Knights, Men-at-Arms and Crossbowmen is a generic European war party rather than a merchant party under Mongol safe-conduct.

title: The Battle of Hastings
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from

  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 2) [path "VC - Harold Slain"]
Defeat:

  - TIMER on 1500s elapsed [path "Defeat - Nightfall"]
issues_found: Elevation grid is uniformly 0 across the whole 120x120 map: there is no Senlac Hill at all, even though the brief, the narration and the 'lure the fyrd down the slope' mechanic all turn on the English holding high ground. This was entirely avoidable in the editor.

A continuous water strip is cut straight across the middle of the map (row ~23 of the 40-row digest). No river or strait figured at Hastings, and a full-width water barrier between the two deployment areas contradicts a battle fought on a single continuous slope.

The dirt band in the north and the surrounding 2400 oak trees make the field a generic forest clearing rather than the open ridge-and-marsh ground of Senlac; the historical field was open cultivated slope, not woodland.

Harold is represented by the KING unit rather than a renamed Champion or infantry hero; the King is a fleeing non-combatant, so the man who fought on foot in the centre of his own shield wall cannot stand in it.
Force proportions favour Norman cavalry over infantry (10 Knights + 6 Light Cavalry vs only 6 Spearmen and 8 Archers), whereas William's infantry contingent was at least as large as his mounted arm.

Nine of ten triggers fire on TIMER, so William's rally, Harold's defiance and the retreat hint all play out identically regardless of what the player does; only the 'Fyrd Lured' event is gated on player action (OBJECTS_IN_AREA).
Both players are given Town Centers, Houses, a Monastery and military production buildings, implying a settled base-building engagement rather than two field armies that met on one afternoon.
strengths: The engine's actual William the Conqueror hero is used for the Norman commander rather than a substitute from another era.
Franks for the Normans and Britons for the Anglo-Saxons are both apt civilizations for 1066 England, with consistent Western European architecture.
The English roster deliberately mirrors the sources: 14 Spearmen as fyrd levies, 6 Champions as housecarls, and only 2 Archers, correctly reflecting Harold's near-total lack of missile troops.

Victory is keyed to the death of Harold (KING, path 'VC - Harold Slain'), the actual decisive event, and defeat to William's death plus a 1500-second nightfall deadline that encodes the real 'break the wall before dark' constraint.
Narration is factually sound: 14 October 1066, the road to London, the shield wall, and the feigned-retreat tactic that drew the levies off the ridge.
justification: The scenario gets the parties, the leaders and the goal right: the genuine William the Conqueror hero leads a cavalry-and-archer Frankish force against a Briton shield wall of 14 spearmen, 6 champions and just 2 archers, and victory is properly keyed to Harold's death against a 25-minute nightfall deadline and William's own survival. But the map is a total failure on the one feature the battle turned on — the elevation grid is flat 0 everywhere, so there is no Senlac Hill for the shield wall to hold or for the fyrd to be lured down, and an unhistorical full-width water strip and 2400 oaks turn the field into a forest clearing. Compounding this, nine of ten triggers are pure timers, so the feigned retreat and the wall's collapse are narrated on a clock rather than earned, with only the 'Fyrd Lured' check responding to the player.

The mine/countermine branch and the two specific defeat conditions are the strongest work here.

issues_found: No Janissaries on the Ottoman side, though the Turks civilization ships them and the narration explicitly promises 'elite infantry'; generic Champions stand in for the Sultan's household corps — an avoidable substitution.
The garrison's 'Spanish arquebusiers' are represented by Crossbowmen and Skirmishers, although Teutons have access to Hand Cannoneers, which would have depicted 1529 firearms far better.

Force scale is tiny and near-symmetrical (~21 defenders vs ~19 besiegers); the historical siege was a garrison of roughly 20,000 against an Ottoman host many times its size, and the roster gives no sense of that disparity.

Victory fires on the destruction of a Player 2 CAMEL_RIDER under a path named only 'Ottoman Withdrawal' — no person or place — so the winning condition is a unit hunt against an ordinary cavalry unit rather than the historical goal of outlasting the siege until the autumn withdrawal.
A survival timer or the destruction of the renamed Suleiman (the KING is present and named by trigger) would have been the correct victory key; the King is left unused as a target.

Map is entirely flat (elevation 0 everywhere) with water confined to a band along the extreme north edge; the Danube arm and the Wien stream that shaped the Ottoman approach and the mining sector at the Carinthian Gate are not represented in the terrain.
3,667 oak trees dominate the object count, implying dense woodland around a city that in 1529 sat amid cleared glacis and suburbs deliberately burned by the defenders.

Assault waves ([E1], [E3], [E5]) are gated on elapsed time rather than on the preceding event, so the sequence plays out largely identically regardless of player action; only the mine/countermine pair is genuinely conditional.
strengths: Civilization assignment is exactly right: Teutons for the German/Austrian garrison and Turks for Suleiman's army, giving period-appropriate architecture for both the walled city and the besiegers' camp.
The city is actually built as a walled place — 82 stone wall segments, a gate, four guard towers, a castle and a Town Center — matching a defence of Vienna's medieval circuit.
The Ottoman camp is rendered with pavilions and tents plus a siege workshop, and the narration correctly notes that the heavy siege cannon lagged in the mud, which is why sapping dominates.

The mine/countermine mechanic is modelled conditionally: a sapping engine brought to the gate breaches it, while destroying it first fires 'Countermine Success' — the genuine turning point of the siege.
Defeat on the loss of the renamed Salm Champion and on the fall of the Town Center encodes the losses the defenders actually faced.
Dates, the Carinthian Gate focus, the mix of Landsknechts and Spanish arquebusiers, and the withdrawal caused by autumn rains and supply failure are all stated accurately.
justification: The scenario gets the frame right — Teutons behind 82 wall segments and a gate, Turks in a tented camp with a siege workshop, and a conditional mine/countermine sequence at the Carinthian Gate that is the real hinge of 1529. It is undermined by avoidable roster choices (no Janissaries despite the Turks having them and the text promising elite infantry; Crossbowmen standing for arquebusiers when Hand Cannoneers exist) and by terrain that is uniformly flat with water only at the far north edge, so the Danube frontage and the mining ground are absent. Most damaging, victory is keyed to destroying a single Player 2 CAMEL_RIDER under a path naming no person, reducing an endurance siege to a unit hunt when the renamed Suleiman KING or a hold timer was available.
